teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a validation order has score 0.60. It is above a candidate threshold 0.50 but below a candidate threshold 0.70, so the resulting class decision differs while the score is unchanged. For each supplied threshold, form labels and count TP, FP, TN and FN on the same validation observations. Calculate conditional error rates and the fixed expected-cost quantity. If the eligible threshold records have costs 0.28 and 0.25, the minimum-cost rule selects 0.25, subject to the declared limits. Retain that threshold before protected testing. The ordinary binary probability cutoff of 0.5 and decision_function cutoff of zero describe different score representations, not two interchangeable numerical settings.

Keep each threshold's decisions separate from its underlying scores. The same 0.60 score illustrates that a different cutoff changes the predicted-positive group and therefore the confusion table. Precision, recall, FPR and FNR must then be recomputed from those resulting decisions rather than copied from another threshold. The supplied minimum-cost comparison uses fixed deployment probabilities and costs throughout. Retain the selected cutoff together with its score representation, validation record and eligibility verdict so later inference and protected testing apply precisely that decision rule.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A score is not already the final class decision. A task threshold changes decisions, and the protected test cannot be used to rescue a threshold that fails the fixed comparison.

media.group_title: Aggregate improvement and uneven slice performance

segments.label: Why overall improvement can hide language-slice gaps
segments.summary: In a synthetic fraud example, true fraud rates are equal across languages, but an English-centric description-quality score is lower for Hindi and Hinglish. Adding that score improves overall detection, with the highest-scoring 10% flagged. Regional flag rates look nearly identical: 9.2% for metro and 9.1% for rural and tier-two regions. Language-level detection tells a different story: the model detects 33.5% of fraud overall, but only about one-fifth of English-language fraud, over 40% of Hindi-language fraud, and more than half of Hinglish-language fraud. Similar regional rates therefore conceal uneven language-slice performance.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the deployment probability of the subgroup is 0.25 and its subgroup-conditional expected harm under the supplied error costs is 0.80. Its contribution to total expected harm is 0.25 × 0.80 = 0.20. If a supplied mitigation changes the subgroup harm to 0.60, the corresponding contribution becomes 0.15 under the same population probability. Still inspect its overall validation evidence and the affected group's representation before accepting it. For any binary-rate calculation, retain the actual-negative and actual-positive denominators separately. The calculation weights conditional harm by population share; it does not turn a small evaluation sample into justified deployment representation.

The multiplication by 0.25 is the population weighting step, not a revision to the subgroup's conditional rate. Keep subgroup false-positive and false-negative conditions distinct when computing its harm. Then compare the supplied mitigation with the reference on a matched affected segment and overall cohort. An improvement in the subgroup contribution is useful evidence only under the supplied population probability and cost assumptions. Inspect representation before extending that evidence to deployment. The exercise is a bounded check of a provided mitigation; it does not authorize inventing protected categories, new policies or an untested repair that merely seems fair.

Suppose the declared seed list yields five completed matched baseline/candidate pairs and the candidate wins three. Its empirical win probability is 3/5 = 0.60 for those trials. segments.label: Recognize overfitting from training and validation loss
segments.summary: Overfitting occurs when a model fits training observations closely but generalizes poorly. A one-input, one-output example illustrates why closely following training values need not capture the underlying pattern. Comparing training and validation loss provides evidence: if training loss continues falling while validation loss rises, the improvement on training data is not carrying over to validation.

bridge_note.before: Watch for the contrast between falling training loss and rising validation loss. Both use a lower-is-better interpretation; a better training result alone does not establish better generalization.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains the overfitting signal, not setting selection, conditional error rates, expected error cost, protected-test safeguards, or estimator-specific penalty direction. The text supplies these rules for choosing regularization.

A supported segment limitation belongs to the evaluation record and should be described at that scope. This separation prevents the record from becoming either a new authorization policy or an unsupported claim of suitability.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose features have shape (4, 2), and the declared targets have shape (4,). Construct tensors from the two NumPy arrays, explicitly convert each to its declared dtype, and inspect the resulting shapes and dtypes. Return the aligned pair as a tuple only after checking the common batch length and required axes. A target fixture with three rows fails correspondence even if each target value is individually permitted. Another fixture can test an incorrect declared target representation without changing the feature dtype. Keeping these checks separate makes it clear whether a failure concerns feature shape, target shape, dtype or matching observations, rather than reporting only that conversion succeeded.

Inspect features and targets separately before checking their common observation axis. A classification target representation may differ from numerical features, so an explicit cast should use the target's declared dtype rather than a shared convenience setting. Return the pair only after the axes and representations satisfy the contract. In the three-target failure fixture, tensor conversion may still succeed; the alignment check is what rejects it. Test that failure alongside an accepted pair and the supplied boundary. This establishes a reliable input contract for later minibatch use without relying on a subsequent loss to expose an earlier conversion error.

teaching_blocks.content: Constructing tensors does not establish their task contract. Target dtype must come from the declared target representation, and equal-looking values do not repair a mismatched batch length.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For five indexed observations and batch_size 2, a fixture with drop_last=False retains batches of sizes 2, 2 and 1. With drop_last=True, it retains two complete batches and discards the incomplete final batch. Retrieve each feature and target from the same observation index in __getitem__, and return them together. Test the batch boundaries and observed pairings under the declared shuffle policy rather than assuming a loader output's first position still corresponds to the source's first row. Also check __len__ against the sample count. The choice about the incomplete batch must appear in the fixture expectations, because counting three batches of size two would invent an observation.

Indexing defines correspondence before batching. If __getitem__ uses the feature at one index and the target at another, a loader can still collate a well-shaped but incorrectly paired batch. Test item identities as well as batch dimensions. The five-observation fixture also exposes the final partial-batch policy: retaining it gives one smaller batch, while dropping it changes how much of the dataset is consumed. Shuffle governs order, not whether a feature and its target remain the same item. Keep these responsibilities distinct so the expected loader output is tied to the dataset contract rather than assumed from its shape alone.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A minibatch loader does not make a partial batch full. Dropping or retaining the final incomplete batch is an explicit policy, and feature/target alignment begins with the dataset item.

context.concept_name: Define a neural network with task-compatible layers and activations

coverage.learning_objective: Build a minimal module whose layer widths, nonlinearity and output shape satisfy the task.

required_facts.statement: Import torch.nn as nn and define an nn.Module subclass with super().__init__(), registered layer attributes and a forward(self, x) method.
nn.Linear(in_features, out_features) maps each input feature vector to out_features outputs using learned weights and bias, preserving the leading minibatch dimension.
nn.ReLU applies max(0, x) elementwise and introduces a nonlinearity between linear layers.
nn.Sequential composes its modules in declared order; match each layer’s output width to the next layer’s input width.
Set the final layer width and activation to the supplied output task contract and verify the resulting output shape with a fixture batch.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a fixture has four observations with two features, and the declared model uses widths 2 → 3 → 1. The first linear layer maps each two-feature vector to three outputs; ReLU applies its elementwise nonlinearity; the final linear layer maps three to one. The expected output shape is (4, 1), preserving the minibatch length. Register layers as attributes in an nn.Module subclass and implement forward, or use the supplied Sequential composition. Verify the final activation against the task contract rather than adding one from habit. A width mismatch between the intermediate output and the next input is a contract problem, not something a different batch size fixes.

Draw or inspect the dimension chain for a single observation and then restore the leading minibatch dimension. Two features enter the first layer, three intermediate values emerge and one final output is produced; all four observations follow the same chain. Registered layer attributes make those layer parameters part of the module. The activation is elementwise, so it changes values without changing that intermediate width. Finally, compare the model output with the declared target/loss contract. The architecture example remains bounded to that contract rather than adding layers or final nonlinearities simply because they appear in another task.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Linear layer widths describe per-observation feature/output dimensions, not the number of observations. The final width and activation come from the supplied task rather than a generic neural-network template.

context.concept_name: Compute neural-network gradients with automatic differentiation

coverage.learning_objective: Verify parameter gradients against the corresponding matrix-shaped derivative reference.

required_facts.statement: Autograd records tensor operations as a computation graph and differentiates the scalar output through that graph using the chain rule.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: Set requires_grad=True on trainable leaf tensors, form the supplied scalar loss, call loss.backward(), and inspect each leaf parameter’s .grad.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: Backward accumulates into .grad, so clear old gradients before comparing a fresh computation with the reference.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#autogradqs_tutorial.html — Tensors, Functions and Computational graph; Computing Gradients

required_facts.statement: Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances.
Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Gradients, Loss and Optimizer
teaching_blocks.content: A scalar loss must send the intended learning signal through the linear computation to its parameters. Autograd's result is inspectable: compare parameter gradients with a matrix-shaped chain-rule reference, not just with an expectation that backward should work.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Autograd records tensor operations as a computation graph and differentiates the scalar output through that graph using the chain rule. Set requires_grad=True on trainable leaf tensors, form the supplied scalar loss, call loss.backward(), and inspect each leaf parameter’s .grad. Backward accumulates into .grad, so clear old gradients before comparing a fresh computation with the reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For a linear batch Z = XW + b with scalar-loss derivative D = ∂L/∂Z, the chain rule yields ∂L/∂W = X.T @ D and ∂L/∂b = D.sum(axis=0), with any loss reduction already included in D. Compare the computed gradients to the matrix-shaped chain-rule reference with explicit relative and absolute tolerances. Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Take X=[[1, 2], [3, 4]] and the supplied derivative D=[[0.1], [0.2]] for Z=XW+b. The weight-gradient reference is X.T @ D = [[0.7], [1.0]], and the bias-gradient reference is [0.3]. Any loss reduction is already included in D; dividing again would change the reference. Set trainable leaf tensors to require gradients, form the scalar loss and call backward. Inspect .grad before clearing it, and compare shapes and values under explicit tolerances. For a fresh computation, clear the old gradients first because backward accumulates. Include a failure fixture whose gradient differs from the declared reference, not only a successful call.

Read the matrix reference one parameter at a time. The first weight combines feature values 1 and 3 with derivatives 0.1 and 0.2, giving 0.7. The second combines 2 and 4 with the same derivatives, giving 1.0. The bias combines derivatives over rows, giving 0.3. These shapes are part of the check: a transpose error can yield a different object even when some scalar values look plausible. Because D includes the loss reduction, use it once as supplied. Compare after backward and before clearing so the inspected gradients correspond to the intended fresh computation rather than zeroed or accumulated state.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Backward does not overwrite every old gradient automatically. A gradient comparison also needs the correct matrix shapes and reduction convention; a numerically plausible scalar is not the weight matrix reference.

context.concept_name: Choose a task-compatible training loss

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a task-compatible loss and verify its output, target and gradient contracts.

required_facts.statement: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective.
source_refs: pytorch_learn_basics#optimization_tutorial.html — Hyperparameters; Loss Function; Optimizer; Full Implementation

required_facts.statement: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C).
MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.
BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs.

For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target.
For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Gradients, Loss and Optimizer
teaching_blocks.content: The model output and target must meet the selected loss's contract. A scalar loss value alone cannot tell you whether class indices, logits, probabilities and same-shaped numerical targets were used correctly.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: A loss compares model outputs with the corresponding target representation; choose its input contract before computing the scalar objective. CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized class logits; for class-index targets, logits have shape (N, C), targets have shape (N,) with dtype long and values in [0, C). MSELoss takes input and target tensors of the same shape and, under mean reduction, averages their squared elementwise differences.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and binary cross-entropy for logits and same-shaped targets in [0, 1], rather than expecting already-sigmoid-transformed inputs. For mean squared error over M output elements, the loss derivative with respect to an output is 2 × (output−target)/M, so its sign points toward increasing loss as the output moves away from the target. For unweighted mean binary cross-entropy with logits over M elements, the logit derivative is (sigmoid(logit)−target)/M; this distinguishes the probability representation from the raw logit.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: For mean class-index cross-entropy without weighting, the derivative per sample logit is (softmax probability−one-hot target)/N, so output width, target identity and reduction affect the gradient reference.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
For an unweighted mean squared-error fixture with outputs [2, 4] and targets [1, 2], the loss is (1²+2²)/2 = 2.5 and output derivatives are [1, 2]. For a binary-logit fixture with one logit 0 and target 1, sigmoid(0)=0.5, so the supplied mean-logit derivative is −0.5. For target 1, decreasing the logit increases loss, while increasing it decreases loss. For a class-index task with three classes, verify logits width 3 and long target indices in [0, 3); use the stated softmax-minus-one-hot reference with its sample-count reduction. These are distinct output contracts, not interchangeable wrappers around arbitrary tensors.

Keep the mean-reduction factor visible in each reference. The two-element MSE fixture divides squared errors by two, while the one-element binary-logit fixture divides its sigmoid-minus-target derivative by one. A class-index cross-entropy reference subtracts the one-hot target from the softmax vector and divides by the sample count. Those equations support different target representations, so verify target dtype and axes before applying them. A positive-looking scalar loss is not proof of the right contract. Compare both value and derivative direction in the bounded fixture, retaining the supplied assumptions about unweighted mean reduction.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: CrossEntropyLoss expects unnormalized logits for the class-index case; BCEWithLogitsLoss also expects logits, not already-sigmoid inputs. MSE's same-shape contract must be checked rather than left to accidental broadcasting.

required_facts.statement: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement.
For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted.
Retain the model weights associated with the best monitored validation value rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.
A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model.
Do not use protected test observations to fit preprocessing, choose a model or tune its settings; doing so leaks information into the chosen system.

teaching_blocks.content:

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Predeclare the validation quantity, improvement direction, minimum improvement and patience; patience counts consecutive epochs without sufficient improvement. For a minimized validation quantity, reset the non-improvement counter only when current < best − min_delta; otherwise increment it and stop when the declared patience is exhausted. Here, best is the validation value at the most recent checkpoint accepted under min_delta, not necessarily the lowest observed value. Retain that accepted checkpoint’s model weights rather than automatically using the last epoch’s weights.

teaching_blocks.content:
A state_dict refers to live parameter values, so preserve a best-epoch state with a deep copy or a saved state file before later updates alter the model. Implement the controller as a while loop bounded by maximum epochs and the non-improvement rule; update best loss/checkpoint inside the improvement branch and use break when patience is exhausted.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose minimized validation values are 0.50, 0.44, 0.43 and 0.45, with min_delta 0.02 and patience 2. The move from 0.50 to 0.44 is sufficient improvement and resets the counter. The value 0.43 does not satisfy 0.43 < 0.44−0.02, so the counter becomes one; 0.45 makes it two and exhausts patience. The lowest observed value is 0.43, but the best checkpoint accepted under min_delta is the one at 0.44. Preserve the 0.44 checkpoint’s weights by deep copy or a saved state file, and restore that checkpoint for subsequent use rather than the last weights. Protected-test observations do not decide patience or checkpoint choice.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.content:
A state_dict reference is not necessarily a frozen best-epoch snapshot. Later updates can alter live parameter values, and ‘slightly lower’ is not sufficient improvement when it fails the declared min_delta rule.

Source for checkpoint reference versus copy: [PyTorch Saving and Loading Models — Save/Load state_dict (Recommended), best_model_state note](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/saving_loading_models.html).

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the derivative reference predicts a negative gradient for a selected parameter, but the reproduced record shows zero. Inspect .grad after backward and before clearing it, then follow the derivative chain from loss through outputs to that parameter. Check the target representation and declared learning rate alongside the loss computation. Choose one supported root-cause hypothesis, apply its supplied correction and rerun the identical bounded fixture. Compare the corrected loss and gradient signs and magnitudes with the failing reference. A lower loss in a different task or with multiple simultaneous changes would not isolate this hypothesis. Keep assertion fixtures for both the expected computation and the reproduced failure.

The identical rerun is what makes the correction test informative. Preserve the fixture, target contract and baseline failing evidence while changing the one supported factor. If the correction is intended to restore a missing gradient path, inspect the derivative and parameter .grad at the same points as before. If the supplied cause concerns representation or learning rate, retain those resolved inputs in the comparison. Record whether the corrected bounded task meets its declared expectations, not just whether an exception disappeared. This isolates evidence for one hypothesis without claiming that all future training failures have the same cause.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A stalled loss does not justify arbitrary configuration changes. Gradient evidence has a timing requirement, and inspecting after zeroing gradients can hide the learning signal you intended to diagnose.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Wrap the measured computation in the PyTorch profiler context and mark data-loading and model-computation regions with record_function labels. Inspect key_averages().table(...) or the trace to attribute elapsed operator and labeled-region work to the observed bottleneck. Warm up the workload before comparing steady-state execution and remove profiler overhead when making the final unprofiled timing comparison.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: CUDA work is asynchronous, so CPU clock timings require synchronization at the measurement boundaries to include completed accelerator work. Change one supported bottleneck factor and compare the same bounded workload again rather than inferring improvement only from a code change. Inspect CPU and memory measurements and running process state during the profiled interval, using docker stats and docker top for a containerized run, to distinguish resource limits from stage timing evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Warm up the bounded workload, then profile its labeled regions. If the trace attributes most measured work to loading, test one supported loading factor rather than immediately changing model computation. Inspect CPU, memory and process state during the same interval; for the container fixture, docker stats and docker top provide that supporting evidence. After the change, compare the same bounded workload again without profiler overhead in the final timing. On CUDA, synchronize measurement boundaries so a CPU clock includes completed accelerator work. Keep the profiling attribution separate from the final unprofiled performance comparison, since they answer related but different questions.

The profiler trace supplies attribution, while the unprofiled rerun supplies the matched elapsed-time comparison. Keep the same bounded workload and one-factor change between those two comparisons. A loading-region label should enclose the intended loading work; a model-compute label should identify that separate work rather than blend it with setup. Runtime CPU, memory and process evidence must refer to the same window. Synchronization at accelerator timing boundaries accounts for asynchronous completion. This makes the observed difference interpretable without assuming that a profiler's overhead or a shifted measurement boundary is a genuine speed improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A code change is not evidence of improvement. Asynchronous accelerator work and profiler overhead can alter timing interpretation unless the measurement boundaries and final comparison are controlled.

teaching_blocks.content:
For the bounded ViT image-classification adaptation, use these explicit imports:

```python
import torch
from torch import nn
from transformers import AutoImageProcessor, ViTForImageClassification, TrainingArguments, Trainer
``` Load the supplied compatible checkpoint with ViTForImageClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint). Retain its original label mapping for the pretrained baseline before replacing the task head. Load the matching processor with AutoImageProcessor.from_pretrained(checkpoint). Calling that processor on images with return_tensors="pt" produces pixel_values; passing the resulting inputs as keyword arguments to the model yields logits through its .logits attribute. segments.label: Guard a Python entry point so imports do not invoke it
segments.summary: Python sets __name__ to "__main__" when it executes a file directly, and to the module's name when another file imports it. The example first leaves a print statement unguarded, showing that importing a module executes its top-level code. It then moves that statement into a main function and places the function call behind if __name__ == "__main__":. Direct execution calls main; importing the same module does not call main. The guard controls the entry-point call, not all code in the imported module.

bridge_note.before: Watch how direct execution and import produce different __name__ values. The creator calls main a method; here it is a function serving as an entry point.
bridge_note.after: The clip establishes the guard, not the training workflow. The text covers parameter defaults and overrides, JSON loading and serialization, notebook comparison, checked subprocess execution, explicit state, f-string reporting, repository commits, and clean-shell output capture.

required_facts.statement: A mutable object name can refer to new contents after an overwrite; Object Versioning retains noncurrent versions whose identities can be selected explicitly.

Retrieve a Google Cloud Storage snapshot with bucket.blob(object_name, generation=recorded_generation).download_to_filename(local_path), preserving the generation instead of resolving the current object.
Use the authorized client to confirm the supplied object/version exists before recording the snapshot as available.
Compute a digest from the actual bytes, for example hashlib.sha256(data_bytes).hexdigest(), and compare it with the recorded expected content identity.
Write the object name, generation and observed digest to the local snapshot record so later training can retrieve and verify the same bytes.
Upload the dataset to the version-enabled bucket with bucket.blob(object_name).upload_from_filename(local_path), then inspect the created object generation and record it.
Read the local dataset through with open(path, "rb") as handle and update the SHA-256 digest from those bytes before recording the upload identity.
After overwriting the mutable latest object in the test bucket, download the originally recorded generation again and compare its digest with the original snapshot digest.

teaching_blocks.content: A dataset name still exists, but its contents have been overwritten. Reproduction requires the recorded object generation and actual content identity, not just a path called latest.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Upload the supplied dataset to the version-enabled test bucket and record its created generation and the SHA-256 digest of the local bytes. Later, select that recorded generation explicitly, verify it exists and download it. Compare the downloaded bytes' digest with the expected snapshot identity. In the authorized overwrite fixture, change only the mutable latest object, then retrieve the original generation again. The observed original digest should still match the snapshot record. Keep object name, generation and digest together: the name tells you which object family, the generation selects the version, and the digest checks the bytes you actually obtained.

The overwrite test separates immutable snapshot selection from the mutable object's current state. Verify the recorded generation exists before relying on it, and check the content after retrieval rather than assuming a version-qualified request returned the expected bytes. A local digest computed before upload and a digest of the later download can be compared directly as content evidence. Keep the selected generation in the record even when both old and latest objects happen to have the same name. The test proves retrieval of the recorded fixture, not a claim that mutable names are intrinsically safe for reproduction.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: A mutable object name is not immutable data identity. Recording a digest without verifying downloaded bytes also does not establish that the intended snapshot was retrieved.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Reproducibility requires exact data identity, not a mutable location.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement a learner-defined Python snapshot function with learner-written imports for hashing, local record handling and the authorized object-storage client. Read the supplied dataset through an explicit binary file handle, compute its SHA-256 digest, upload it to the supplied version-enabled test bucket, and confirm the created generation exists. Write the object name, generation and digest to a local record through an explicit file handle. Retrieve that exact generation and verify its digest, then repeat the retrieval and verification after the authorized fixture overwrites the mutable latest object.
practice_anchor.success: The local record contains the uploaded object name, its confirmed generation and the digest of the original dataset bytes. Both generation-qualified downloads match that digest, including the download performed after the latest object changes.

live_code.required_skill: Define a Python function that uses imported libraries, explicit file handles and an authorized storage client to create and verify an exact dataset snapshot.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Supply the original local training dataset, an existing authorized client runtime, a version-enabled test bucket, an object name, local record and download paths, and replacement bytes for the authorized latest-object overwrite fixture. Provide the function contract and acceptance expectations, but no complete implementation.
live_code.observable_success: The learner's function imports its dependencies, hashes the original bytes read through an explicit file handle, uploads the dataset, confirms the exact generation exists and persists its identity through an explicit record file handle. The recorded generation remains unchanged, and its downloaded digest matches the original before and after the overwrite; the replacement bytes produce a different digest.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the recorded object name, original generation and expected SHA-256 digest visible beside the mutable object's current generation. Show matching digests for the original-generation downloads before and after the overwrite, alongside the replacement content's different digest.

coverage.learning_objective: Serialize and verify the actual revision, dependency pins and runtime identity in one manifest.

required_facts.statement: Inspect the actual local repository commit using git rev-parse --verify HEAD and include that exact revision in the environment dictionary.
Collect installed pinned dependency versions with python -m pip freeze, whose package==version output can be installed with pip install -r.
Use imported runtime/environment facilities and the recorded runtime identity to capture the actual execution context alongside the revision and dependency versions.
source_refs: python_tutorial#stdlib.html — Operating System Interface; Command Line Arguments

required_facts.statement: With import json, serialize the manifest dictionary using json.dump(manifest, handle), then parse it using json.load(handle) from the saved file.
source_refs: python_tutorial#inputoutput.html — Saving structured data with json

required_facts.statement: Write and read the manifest with explicit with open(path, "w"/"r", encoding="utf-8") handles.
Compare the parsed revision, dependency-version mapping and runtime identity with independently inspected values and reject a mismatch.
Use import sys to record sys.version and sys.executable as actual Python runtime details alongside the supplied runtime identity.

teaching_blocks.content: The run's environment record should describe what actually executed. A remembered dependency list or a typed commit label is not independent evidence of the Python runtime and repository revision used.

teaching_blocks.content: Inspect the actual local repository commit using git rev-parse --verify HEAD and include that exact revision in the environment dictionary. Use imported runtime/environment facilities and the recorded runtime identity to capture the actual execution context alongside the revision and dependency versions.

teaching_blocks.content: With import json, serialize the manifest dictionary using json.dump(manifest, handle), then parse it using json.load(handle) from the saved file. teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Use import sys to record sys.version and sys.executable as actual Python runtime details alongside the supplied runtime identity.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the local HEAD, collect pinned dependency versions with pip freeze, and record sys.version and sys.executable with the supplied runtime identity. Serialize that dictionary to the declared text manifest and parse it back. Compare the parsed revision, dependency mapping and runtime identity with independently inspected values. If the manifest says revision A but HEAD is B, reject the match rather than correcting the observed revision to fit the manifest. The dependency file can be installed with pip install -r in the declared environment. Keep the saved manifest and verified values identifiable so a later reproduction can resolve the recorded context.

The parsed manifest is the artifact a later execution will read, so inspect it after serialization rather than only inspecting the in-memory dictionary that preceded writing. Compare its dependency mapping with the freeze output, its revision with HEAD and its Python/runtime fields with the actual process. Paths such as sys.executable help identify which interpreter executed, while sys.version records that interpreter's version information. Keep these values beside the environment identity instead of treating them as substitutes for it. A mismatch is a verification failure to resolve, not a reason to change the independently observed environment values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Writing a manifest is not verifying it. Runtime details and dependency pins must come from the actual environment, and a parsed record with a mismatch cannot be declared accurate.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Executable provenance binds code and dependency versions to a model.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement a Python function that inspects the supplied local repository revision, installed pinned dependencies and actual Python runtime, records them alongside the supplied runtime identity, and writes an environment manifest as JSON. Read the saved manifest and verify its values against a fresh, independent inspection.
practice_anchor.success: The saved file parses as JSON and contains the exact local HEAD revision, installed dependency-version mapping, supplied runtime identity, sys.version and sys.executable. Verification accepts matching values and rejects a mismatch without altering independently inspected values.

live_code.observable_success: A fresh inspection of HEAD, dependency pins, runtime identity and Python runtime details matches the parsed saved manifest. Changing a saved revision or dependency version causes verification to raise a mismatch error, while the independently observed values remain unchanged.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the environment inspection, manifest dictionary, explicit JSON write/read handles and parsed-value comparisons visible together, including acceptance of a matching record and rejection of a changed revision or dependency pin.

coverage.learning_objective: Re-execute a recorded experiment in a clean process using its recorded source, inputs and environment.

required_facts.statement: Check out the recorded local repository commit and verify HEAD, rather than running a changed working tree and calling it reproduction.
Download the recorded dataset generation and verify its identity instead of resolving the mutable latest object.
Use the recorded Python/dependency environment, installing its pinned requirements where needed.

required_facts.statement: Redirect shell output with > capture.log 2>&1 to capture standard output and error, and inspect the captured file; a pipe connects the first command’s output to the next command’s input.

teaching_blocks.title: Reproduce a Training Experiment
teaching_blocks.content: To reproduce an experiment, resolve its recorded code, data, environment and settings before execution. Running today's working tree on the current dataset may be another experiment, even if it has the old run's name.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Retrieve the recorded experiment’s revision, dataset snapshot, environment and resolved run settings before executing it again. Check out the recorded local repository commit and verify HEAD, rather than running a changed working tree and calling it reproduction. Download the recorded dataset generation and verify its identity instead of resolving the mutable latest object.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Use the recorded Python/dependency environment, installing its pinned requirements where needed. Define the execution function with default argument values and explicit keyword overrides, and pass the resolved run state through its parameters. Run the script in a clean subprocess using its recorded working directory, checking the process exit result and capturing its output.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Navigate the referenced repository and artifact directories before resolving relative dataset, configuration and script paths. Redirect shell output with > capture.log 2>&1 to capture standard output and error, and inspect the captured file; a pipe connects the first command’s output to the next command’s input.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Retrieve the run's commit and dataset generation. Check out and verify the recorded local commit, download and verify the recorded snapshot, and use the pinned Python/dependency environment. Resolve defaults and keyword overrides through the execution function's parameters. Navigate to the recorded directories before resolving relative script or artifact paths, then launch a clean subprocess with captured output and checked exit status. Inspect the captured result rather than assuming launch means completion. In a failure fixture, a changed latest dataset or different working directory should be distinguishable from the recorded execution context. A shell pipe connects one command's output to another's input; it is not the same operation as saving both output streams to a log.

Compare captured resolved parameters with the run record as well as inspecting exit success. A process can exit successfully while using a wrong dataset or default setting, so the reproduction verdict needs identity and configuration checks too. Relative paths are interpreted from the actual working directory; navigate explicitly before invoking the recorded script. The pinned environment and recorded code commit govern which implementation runs, while the verified snapshot governs its inputs. These separate pieces make the bounded reproduction auditable instead of relying on an operator's memory of the previous notebook session.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: The same script filename is not reproduction identity. A changed revision, mutable dataset or unresolved local path can change the executed experiment despite a familiar name.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Reproduction re-executes an identified experiment rather than approximating it from memory.

practice_anchor.objective: Rerun the supplied recorded experiment using its repository revision, verified dataset generation, pinned environment and resolved settings. Write the required imports and a learner-defined execution function with defaults and explicit keyword overrides. Navigate the recorded directories, check out and verify the recorded local commit, execute the script in a clean subprocess, and capture and inspect shell output using redirection and a pipe.
practice_anchor.success: The rerun uses the verified recorded commit, dataset generation, environment, working directory and resolved settings. The subprocess exit result and captured output are inspected, both shell output streams are saved to capture.log, and a pipe is used to inspect captured content. The reproduction verdict compares the recorded outcome and rerun outcome within the fixture's declared stochastic tolerances; successful process exit alone is not accepted as proof.

context.concept_name: Register a model version from a tracked training run

coverage.learning_objective: Register and verify an artifact’s immutable object version, hash and originating run.

required_facts.statement: Resolve the originating tracked run’s artifact record, expected hash and immutable object version before creating a model registry version.
source_refs: mlflow_docs#ml/tracking/tracking-api/ — Starting and Managing Runs; Logging Data to Runs; Querying Runs Programmatically

required_facts.statement: Download the recorded artifact generation with bucket.blob(key, generation=recorded_generation).download_to_filename(path), not the current object at key.
Compute SHA-256 over the downloaded artifact bytes and reject a mismatch against the run record before registration.

Before version creation, require the supplied model name to exist as a registered model (for a new name, client.create_registered_model(name) creates it); then call client.create_model_version(name=name, source=version_qualified_source, run_id=run_id) and retain its returned numeric version.
Preserve the exact object version and hash in that version’s metadata/tags with set_model_version_tag, so the registry record identifies more than a mutable object name.
source_refs: mlflow_docs#ml/model-registry/workflow/ — Registering a Model; Fetching an MLflow Model from the Model Registry; Deploy and Organize Models

required_facts.statement: Retrieve the created record using get_model_version(name, version), and retrieve its linked originating run to verify the recorded identities.
source_refs: mlflow_docs#ml/model-registry/workflow/ — Registering a Model; Fetching an MLflow Model from the Model Registry; Deploy and Organize Models

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a tracked run records artifact generation A while the mutable key now resolves to B. Download A explicitly and verify its hash before registering. Use the supplied registered model name, creating that name only if the declared new-name path requires it. Return one keyed verdict binding run, version and artifact, instead of treating a later mutable overwrite as a newly approved version.

context.concept_name: Package a versioned model with fitted preprocessing and inference dependencies

coverage.learning_objective: Package fitted preprocessing and model state with dependencies and verify container-reloaded predictions.

required_facts.statement:
Persist the fitted model and fitted preprocessor together using a package path tied to the recorded version:
import pickle
with open(package_path, "wb") as handle:
    pickle.dump({"model": model, "preprocessor": preprocessor}, handle, protocol=5)
source_refs: scikit_learn_user_guide#https://scikit-learn.org/stable/model_persistence.html — 11.4 Using pickle, joblib, or cloudpickle; 11.5 Security & Maintainability Limitations

required_facts.statement:
Reload only a trusted, verified package in the compatible pinned inference environment:
with open(package_path, "rb") as handle:
    package = pickle.load(handle)
model = package["model"]
preprocessor = package["preprocessor"]
Pickle loading can execute arbitrary code and is unsafe for untrusted artifacts.
source_refs: scikit_learn_user_guide#https://scikit-learn.org/stable/model_persistence.html — 11.4 Using pickle, joblib, or cloudpickle; 11.5 Security & Maintainability Limitations

required_facts.statement: Write Dockerfile instructions FROM <compatible-python-image>, WORKDIR /app, COPY requirements.txt ./, RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt, COPY <package-path-in-context> /app/<package-filename>, COPY <serving-source-in-context> /app/<serving-source>, and CMD ["<serving-command>", "<argument>"]; replace placeholders with the declared package, inference dependencies and serving entry point so the default command loads that package.

Run docker build -t IMAGE:TAG CONTEXT to build and tag the package image; CONTEXT must contain the Dockerfile (or select it with -f) and every source used by COPY, with needed files not excluded by .dockerignore; record the resulting immutable image identity as well as its tag.
source_refs: docker_docs#https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/buildx/build/ — Usage; Specify a Dockerfile; Tag an image
docker_docs#docker-concepts/building-images/build-tag-and-publish-an-image — Build an image; Tag an image

required_facts.statement: The packaged prediction path must apply the fitted training preprocessing before the packaged model, not refit preprocessing at inference time.
Use docker run --name NAME -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT --env KEY=VALUE IMAGE to start the referenced image with the declared port and nonsecret runtime settings.
source_refs: docker_docs#https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/container/run/ — Publish or expose port; Set environment variables; Specify a container name

required_facts.statement: Inspect the named container with docker container inspect NAME to check its image identity and State fields.
Use docker container logs NAME to inspect its captured standard output and error for initialization or execution failures.
Do not embed secrets in Dockerfile ARG or ENV instructions, because they persist in the final image or its metadata.
Supply sensitive values through the runtime secret mechanism rather than placing their literal values in the Compose configuration.
Save and reload the fitted model/preprocessor through explicit binary file handles, and write/read the pinned dependency manifest through a text file handle.
Record pinned inference package versions in the package’s requirements manifest and install that manifest in the serving image.
Assert the pre-save and container-reloaded predictions agree on the same fixed inputs under declared tolerances, and separately check that fitted preprocessing parameters are preserved.
Write assert predicate checks for the declared valid, boundary and failure cases; a false predicate raises AssertionError during ordinary non-optimized execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Register and Package the Model
teaching_blocks.content: The serving package needs the fitted model and its fitted preprocessor together. A container that loads only weights or refits preprocessing can execute successfully without reproducing the intended prediction representation.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Persist the fitted model and preprocessor together in the recorded version-tied package path. Import pickle, open that path with a binary "wb" handle and call pickle.dump on the dictionary {"model": model, "preprocessor": preprocessor}, passing the handle and protocol=5. Reload only a trusted, verified package in the compatible pinned inference environment. Open the package path with a binary "rb" handle and call pickle.load on that handle. Retrieve the model and preprocessor from the corresponding dictionary keys. Pickle loading can execute arbitrary code and is unsafe for untrusted artifacts. The Dockerfile uses FROM for the compatible Python image, WORKDIR /app, COPY requirements.txt ./ and RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt. COPY the package and serving source from the declared build context into their declared /app paths. Set CMD to the declared serving command and argument as a JSON array, so the default command loads this package. teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose validation selected candidate B and its threshold, and the protected cohort contains a different observed class mix. Predict that cohort with B and the baseline on the same observations. Use the already fixed deployment probabilities and error costs, not new values chosen to make B pass. Check the precommitted quality and operating requirements and retain the test's actual-class conditioning counts. If B fails the requirement, report failure. A threshold adjustment based on these test outcomes would let the protected observations choose the system, contradicting the boundary. The output is a final matched comparison, not another candidate-selection round.

Freeze means the choices are made before test outcomes are observed: model identity, fitted preprocessing, threshold, metric inputs and requirements all retain their declared values. The baseline and candidate predictions then use the same protected observations for a final matched comparison. Retain the test's observed conditioning counts while applying the supplied deployment probabilities; these are different roles in the calculation. If a required quantity is undefined or a requirement fails, report that outcome explicitly. This protects the interpretation of final testing rather than using it as a source of additional tuning information.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Protected testing is not a second tuning opportunity. Test failure does not authorize switching candidate, refitting preprocessing or searching for a better threshold on those observations.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the request contract permits a two-feature matrix with one row per order. A body decoding to three rows of two permitted values can be checked for rank and width, then the response must have the declared row alignment. A body missing a required key fails before prediction. A numeric boundary fixture can test an included limit and a value just beyond it. Send the serialized body as encoded bytes with the declared JSON header and a bounded timeout, decode the returned JSON and inspect its fields. Parsing success, request validity and response correctness are three different checks; retain each failure explicitly rather than returning a successful result for malformed input.

The schema checks must happen before using a field as model input. Check that the required key exists, that its value has the declared type and that its dimensions and values satisfy the stated predicates. A missing key and an out-of-range value are different rejected fixtures. After prediction, inspect the structured response independently: required output keys, row correspondence and declared value or shape expectations. Bounded request timing is part of the fixture transport, not a substitute for contract validation. Explicit rejection distinguishes invalid input from a successful prediction containing the wrong data.

teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose five keyed orders are processed in chunks of two, two and one. Apply the fitted preprocessing and model to each chunk, keeping each order key with its prediction. Write that bounded set of serialized results before reading the next chunk. Decode the written fixture again and verify its schema and one-result-per-eligible-key correspondence. A missing key or duplicate output is a failure even if the total number of rows looks reasonable. Keep explicit input and output handles and the declared reader format. The procedure is inference over chunks, not fitting a new model or preprocessor for whichever chunk happens to arrive next.

Keep an output key beside its prediction through serialization, not merely in a temporary input structure. After writing, decode the fixture and compare key coverage against the eligible input IDs. A duplicate result for A plus a missing result for B could leave the total row count unchanged, which is why correspondence needs more than counting rows. Each chunk uses the same fitted objects and declared response schema. The bounded writer and reader handles establish where results were produced and re-inspected. This completes an inference path whose correctness includes persistence and identity, not only in-memory prediction values.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Sustainable serving capacity is successful completed work per unit time under a specified sustained load profile, bounded latency and failure rate; offered request rate alone is not throughput.

practice_anchor.objective: Run and inspect the supplied prediction-service image with a published HTTP port and declared nonsecret settings. Record outcomes, completed-request latency and backlog throughout each window, calculate the required statistics, and evaluate each load against predeclared acceptance limits.
practice_anchor.success: Container identity, State fields and logs are inspected. Fixture assertions verify successful predictions and declared invalid-request rejections. Each measured load reports attempted requests, successful completions, HTTP errors, timeouts, other failures, unfinished work, successful completions per second, success probability and failed-request fraction. Completed-request latency reports mean, standard deviation and the declared percentile with sample count, units and calculation conventions. The final report identifies the highest measured successful throughput satisfying the required throughput, tail-latency, success and error limits with stable backlog throughout the window, or states that no measured load is feasible.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose one request starts at time 1.0, waits until 1.4 for its batch and completes at 1.6. Its end-to-end duration is 0.6 seconds, not the 0.2-second post-wait interval. Decode the successful response and associate it with the request identity and batching setting. Compute the declared tail percentile, mean and specified spread over the eligible successful-response durations in one unit. Compare settings using the same trace and population interpretation, then choose only a limit satisfying the supplied latency objective. Keep the successful-response sample count visible rather than treating a duration list as if it included failures or unmatched responses.

Use a timeline for the same identified request to avoid measuring different intervals under different settings. Start-to-response timing includes the waiting interval, and the selected successful-response population determines which durations enter the percentile. Record the sample count, units and percentile convention so the numerical summary is reproducible. A limit that reduces model-execution time but increases waiting may fail the full latency objective. The supplied trace is evidence about those measured settings and eligible responses; it does not authorize inventing an unmeasured batching configuration or treating unmatched responses as valid duration samples.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Batch waiting belongs in the stated end-to-end latency. A faster execution interval alone does not make a batching limit acceptable under the full request objective.

video_need.reason: A request timeline makes waiting and execution contributions to end-to-end latency visible.

practice_anchor.success: Only matched successful responses enter the duration arrays. Durations include batch waiting. Each setting's results state the successful-response sample count, unit, percentile convention, mean and standard-deviation divisor. The selected batching limit satisfies the supplied tail-latency objective under the same trace and population interpretation.

No network calls or runtime changes are needed.

context.concept_name: Distinguish data drift, concept drift and observed quality degradation

coverage.learning_objective: Distinguish input shift, changed target relationship and label-supported quality degradation.

required_facts.statement: Input data drift is a change in the observed input distribution relative to its reference; input drift monitoring alone does not measure labeled prediction quality.
Concept drift changes the conditional target relationship P(Y|X), that is, the relationship between features and labels; a previously useful model can become less useful as that relationship changes.
Observed model quality degradation requires comparing predictions with corresponding ground-truth labels and the declared quality reference.
Without matched available labels, report the supported distribution or service evidence and the unresolved quality question rather than asserting labeled quality degradation.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Input data drift is a change in the observed input distribution relative to its reference; input drift monitoring alone does not measure labeled prediction quality. Concept drift changes the conditional target relationship P(Y|X), that is, the relationship between features and labels; a previously useful model can become less useful as that relationship changes. Observed model quality degradation requires comparing predictions with corresponding ground-truth labels and the declared quality reference.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Without matched available labels, report the supported distribution or service evidence and the unresolved quality question rather than asserting labeled quality degradation. teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a production window contains more long-distance orders than the reference. That is evidence about P(X), the input distribution. It does not establish that P(Y|X), the target relationship conditional on features, changed. To claim observed quality degradation, compare predictions with their corresponding ground truth and the declared quality reference. If matched available labels are absent, record the supported distribution or service observation and the unresolved quality question. Conversely, a conditional target relationship can change in the concept-drift sense even when an input summary is not the evidence that reveals it. Keep the three questions distinct rather than calling every change ‘the model got worse.’

Separate an operational report into what is observed and what is unresolved. More long-distance inputs support an input-distribution statement. Matched labels compared with the quality reference support an observed-error statement. Conditional-target evidence addresses whether the feature/label relationship changed. The absence of labels does not prove that quality stayed constant; it means the labeled-quality question is not yet measured by that evidence. Likewise, input drift does not prove that quality worsened. Keeping these distinctions preserves uncertainty without discarding useful distribution or service evidence, and prevents a response justified by one type of evidence from being mislabeled as another.

teaching_blocks.content: Input drift alone is not labeled quality degradation. Changes in P(X), P(Y|X) and matched-label errors do not logically establish one another.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the candidate has lower expected cost than the incumbent but fails a required slice check. Reject it under the fixed gate policy. Calculate both costs with the same supplied deployment probabilities, error costs and actual-class conditional rates. A missing conditioning group does not provide a defined rate. Keep protected-test observations out of fitting and setting choice. Bind the exact registry/artifact identity and verdict to the controlled promotion record, with assertion fixtures for accepted, boundary and failed cases. Approval evidence for candidate A must not be reused for candidate B just because both came from the same retraining pipeline.

The incumbent and candidate must be evaluated under the same fixed validation question before their expected costs are comparable. Keep quality, required slices and deployment compatibility as separately named gate results. A cost improvement does not erase a compatibility failure, and a complete gate record for one identity cannot be transferred to another. Accepted, boundary and rejected fixtures should verify both verdict and identity binding. Promotion evidence therefore states which exact candidate passed which requirements, rather than merely saying that the latest retraining run produced a model with a better number.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Retrained does not mean accepted. An aggregate gain cannot bypass a required slice or compatibility gate, and validation of one artifact does not approve another.

Inspect instance identity, state and process/service evidence and retain the fault record. Under the approved identity, stop the same authorized instance, wait, start it and wait until running. Reconnect and inspect the restored model service. Verify readiness and a bounded prediction exchange against the expected contract rather than assuming a running VM means recovery. Keep credentials in the existing runtime mechanism and out of commands, configuration and captured output. Record state before and after the action. This is a runbook-scoped nonproduction fixture, not permission to restart unrelated resources or broaden the recovery policy.

The pre-recovery evidence is important because stop/start can change process state and remove the immediate fault symptom. Inspect the authorized instance before acting, record what failed and test the runbook's supported hypothesis. After start completes, reconnect and compare model-service state and endpoint behavior with the expected contract. A running instance state is a lifecycle observation; readiness and a successful bounded prediction are service observations. Retain both in the same recovery record along with authorized target identity. This verifies the supplied recovery procedure without assuming that a restart of an arbitrary resource would be safe or sufficient.

teaching_blocks.title: Control Workload Cost and Retire Resources
teaching_blocks.content: Retired resources can be cleaned up only after ownership and release status are verified. An old-looking container may still reference active artifacts, so age alone is not a safe authorization rule.

teaching_blocks.title: The working rule
teaching_blocks.content: Authorize cleanup against the retired-resource inventory and permitted identity scope, preserving the active release rather than selecting resources by age alone. Inspect actual container labels and compare ownership and release/version metadata with the approved active and retired inventory. Inspect each candidate container’s identity and State.Running/exit state; inspect its logs and associated compute lifecycle before deciding it is exclusively retired.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Check captured commands and logs for secret values or sensitive data, with runtime-injected credentials kept out of cleanup code and printed output. Stop only a verified retired container with docker container stop NAME, then remove that stopped retired container with docker container rm NAME. Terminate only the verified exclusively retired nonproduction instance with gcloud compute instances delete INSTANCE --zone=ZONE under the approved disk-preservation policy.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Preserve the active release’s referenced images and required model/preprocessing artifacts; removing a retired container is not authorization to delete shared artifacts. Verify the active serving release remains healthy with a bounded readiness/prediction check, and inspect the inventory to confirm approved retired resources are absent. Write one audit record containing verified ownership, active/retired identities, authorized actions, retained artifacts and credential non-disclosure checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Apply and verify
teaching_blocks.content: Before deleting the verified exclusively retired nonproduction instance, use gcloud compute instances describe INSTANCE --zone=ZONE in the approved project to inspect its status and identity against the verified retired inventory. After the authorized deletion, wait for the deletion operation to complete and check that it completed successfully without errors. Then repeat describe for the same project, zone and instance. Accept only a not-found response for that specific instance as evidence of absence; authentication, permission or other failures are inconclusive or failed verification, not proof that the instance is gone.

teaching_blocks.title: A bounded work example
teaching_blocks.content: Compare actual container labels, identities, running/exit state and logs with the approved active/retired inventory and compute lifecycle. Stop and remove only a verified retired container. Before deleting the exclusively retired nonproduction instance, describe it in the approved project and zone and check its status and identity against the verified retired inventory. Delete only that instance under the approved disk-preservation policy, wait for the deletion operation to complete and check that it succeeded without errors. Repeat describe for the same project, zone and instance: only that instance's not-found response establishes absence; authentication, permission or other failures leave verification inconclusive or failed. Preserve active image references and required model/preprocessing artifacts, even if retired containers also used them. Afterward, verify the active release's readiness and bounded prediction and inspect that the approved retired resources are absent. Write one audit record of ownership, authorized actions, retained artifacts and credential non-disclosure checks. Keep runtime credentials out of cleanup code and captured logs.

teaching_blocks.title: A distinction to keep
teaching_blocks.content: Removing a retired container is not authorization to delete shared artifacts. Cleanup follows verified ownership, permitted scope and lifecycle state while preserving the active serving release.

video_need.reason: A live fixture with visible intermediate state and acceptance checks would make this distinction concrete: Cleanup follows ownership and lifecycle state, not age alone.

practice_anchor.objective: Clean one supplied nonproduction serving-resource inventory using the authorized identity and runtime-injected credentials. Reconcile actual container ownership labels, release identities, running/exit state, logs and compute lifecycle with the approved inventory. Stop and remove only verified retired containers, and describe then delete only the exclusively retired test instance under the approved disk-preservation policy. Preserve the active release and its required images and artifacts, verify health and retired-resource absence, and deliver one safe-cleanup audit record.
practice_anchor.success: Only authorized, verified retired resources are removed. The instance deletion operation completes successfully, and a repeated describe in the same project and zone returns not-found for that specific instance; other failures do not count as absence. The active release passes bounded readiness and prediction checks, its referenced images and required artifacts remain available, and the audit record documents ownership, identities, actions, retained artifacts and credential non-disclosure checks.

Configure inspection and captured output to protect credentials and sensitive data.
live_code.observable_success: Captured evidence links each removal to verified ownership and retirement authorization. The retired containers are absent, the approved instance deletion succeeds and its repeated describe returns the expected instance-specific not-found response, and the active release remains healthy with required artifacts retained. Cleanup code and captured commands/logs disclose no credentials or sensitive data. One audit record contains all required evidence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the approved inventory and inspected runtime evidence visible together: ownership, active/retired identity, container labels, running/exit state, log findings, compute lifecycle, permitted action, retained artifact references and verification result. Distinguish confirmed instance-specific absence from authentication, permission or other verification failures.
